questions.q: State the formula for average velocity and average speed, including their SI units. Explain in one sentence why average speed is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of average velocity.
questions.a: Average velocity v_avg = Δx/Δt = (x₂ - x₁)/(t₂ - t₁), SI unit m/s (vector). Average speed = total path length / Δt, SI unit m/s (scalar). Average speed ≥ |v_avg| because path length ≥ |displacement| by triangle inequality; equality holds only when motion is unidirectional without turning back. A wrong answer (e.g., giving same formula for both, or stating speed = |v_avg| always) reveals confusion between displacement and distance, or between vector and scalar quantities.

questions.q: A car travels 60 km north in 1 hour, then 40 km south in 1 hour. Without calculating, explain whether the magnitude of average velocity equals the average speed for this trip. What physical principle determines the answer?
questions.a: Magnitude of average velocity ≠ average speed. The car reverses direction, so displacement = 20 km north while path length = 100 km. Since path length > |displacement|, average speed > |average velocity|. The principle: displacement is the vector sum of segments (can cancel), while path length is the scalar sum (always adds). A student who says they are equal is ignoring the direction change and treating displacement as total distance.

questions.q: A cyclist rides from home to school 3 km away at 10 km/h, finds school closed, and immediately rides back home at 15 km/h. Calculate (a) average velocity for the full trip, (b) average speed for the full trip, (c) average speed for the first 30 minutes only. Show all steps with units.
questions.a: (a) Displacement = 0 (returns to start), Δt = 3/10 + 3/15 = 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.5 h. v_avg = 0/0.5 = 0 km/h. (b) Total path = 6 km, speed_avg = 6 km / 0.5 h = 12 km/h = 3.33 m/s. (c) First 30 min = 0.5 h. In 0.3 h he reaches school (3 km), then rides back for 0.2 h at 15 km/h covering 3 km. Total path in 0.5 h = 6 km. speed_avg = 6/0.5 = 12 km/h. A wrong answer (e.g., averaging 10 and 15 to get 12.5 km/h) reveals the common error of taking arithmetic mean of speeds instead of total distance/total time.

questions.q: An x-t graph shows a particle at x=0 at t=0, moving to x=10 m at t=2 s, then reversing to x=4 m at t=5 s. Determine (a) average velocity for 0 to 5 s, (b) average speed for 0 to 5 s, (c) the time interval(s) where average velocity equals average speed. Justify using the graph's geometry.
questions.a: (a) Δx = 4 - 0 = 4 m, Δt = 5 s → v_avg = 4/5 = 0.8 m/s (positive). (b) Path = 10 m (forward) + 6 m (backward) = 16 m → speed_avg = 16/5 = 3.2 m/s. (c) Only intervals where motion is unidirectional: 0-2 s (v_avg = speed_avg = 5 m/s) and 2-5 s (v_avg = -6/3 = -2 m/s, speed_avg = 2 m/s, magnitudes equal). A student who says 0-5 s has equal magnitudes is not recognizing the direction reversal visible as a slope sign change on the graph.

questions.q: A student solves: "A man walks 2 km at 4 km/h, then 2 km at 6 km/h. Average speed = (4+6)/2 = 5 km/h." Evaluate this solution. Is it correct? If not, identify the error and give the correct average speed.
questions.a: The solution is incorrect. The error: averaging speeds arithmetically works only when time intervals are equal, not when distances are equal. Correct method: t₁ = 2/4 = 0.5 h, t₂ = 2/6 = 1/3 h. Total distance = 4 km, total time = 5/6 h. speed_avg = 4 / (5/6) = 24/5 = 4.8 km/h. The arithmetic mean (5 km/h) overestimates because more time is spent at the lower speed. A student who defends the arithmetic mean is confusing "average of speeds" with "average speed" — a fundamental definitional error.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using only a stopwatch, a measuring tape, and a toy car on a straight track to demonstrate that average speed can be non-zero while average velocity is zero. Describe the procedure, measurements, and calculations.
questions.a: Procedure: Mark start point O. Run car from O to point A (1 m away), immediately reverse and return to O. Measure total time t_total with stopwatch. Measure OA = 1 m with tape. Calculations: displacement = 0 → v_avg = 0. Path length = 2 m → speed_avg = 2/t_total > 0. A good answer includes repetition for reliability and unit conversion to m/s. A poor answer (e.g., only measuring one-way time, or not reversing) shows failure to grasp that zero displacement requires returning to start, and that speed requires total path length.
